titleStmt.title: Interview with Milton M. Moncrief, April 5, 2004
titleStmt.author: Thomas A. Swope

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Milton M. Moncrief was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Milton M. Moncrief. Mr. Moncrief served in the U.S. Army with the Sixth Armored Division, Ninth Battalion, Company B. He served in the European theater, and he was a prisoner of war. His highest rank was corporal. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Moncrief's home in North Royalton, Ohio, on April 5th, 2004. Mr. Moncrief's wife was also present, and Milt was 80 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Canton, Ohio? How old were you in '41?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: In '41 I was probably about sixteen.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Still in high school at the time, then?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Tell me what you remember about that day.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, I remember the -- the holocaust, disaster, in Pearl Harbor. And then -- that was on a Sunday. Thomas A. Swope:: Right. How -- how did you get the news?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Oh, well, we heard it on the radio. But then Monday morning our school had an assembly; at third period was an open study, or assembly. We were all called in the assembly, and they made the announcement, and they had the radio on about Roosevelt's declaration of war and so forth. So I -- I graduated in '42.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard the news that the war had started for us?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: It -- it was unbelievable, you know, how they could do such a thing as that. It was hard to believe. But the more you heard, you knew it was the facts, you know. And I graduated in '42, and I knew I'd be called. But I got a job, made a little spending money, and then I -- I worked about eight, ten months, and I got my card in April -- yeah; April of '43 I was in the service.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Your job was a regular job? Were you working for the war effort or anything?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, I tried to get in Diebold Safe and Lock.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, at the time they -- you filled out a form, and they'd say, well, they'll call you. Well, I went to Republic Steel, and I was working the same day. Then Diebold called me, but I was either working or sleeping, because at the steel mill you work all shifts. My mother said I was working or something. And they said, well, if he's working at this government job, you know... But when I got my draft card, it wasn't a government job, so --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right. You didn't get a deferment for working in the --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: -- no, no, no, no. I -- I wouldn't have wanted one.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I never even thought of it at that time. No, I -- I went, and I was glad to go. I was a --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you went in, in April of '43, then?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I -- well, we went to Fort Hayes, Columbus. Next day we shipped out. I didn't know where we were going. We ended up in Camp Polk, Louisiana, and that was on Easter Sunday.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And as the guys marched about two miles from the train stop to our area, they were passing out from the heat. They had ODs on, and... This is my wife, Sally.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's all right. When you first reported for -- for basic training, or reported for induction, was it a tough adjustment for you to be there with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: No. I didn't think it was.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Of course, a lot of them were from Kentucky.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And I have a lot of friends from Kentucky.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: The outfit was made up mostly from Ohio, a little West Virginia, and -- the fifth district, you know. And part of Kentucky; Indiana.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, we were in a separate battalion, the 535th Armored Infantry Battalion. They had two of them at Camp Polk, 535th, 536th. And it came on to the fall of the year -- well, in September we had furlough, but then we had additional training, because this was a motorized outfit. We had half-tracks; we had to learn to drive those and all. Of course, you had regular drivers, but you needed backup systems, you know. And it was said that they flipped a coin, but I don't know. I think it was the fact that we were only about half-strength in our battalion. The 535th went to California and joined the Sixth Armored Division. Where the 536th, I think they had more people in there; they went to the South Pacific. They went right over. So we trained about a month in California, and then we shipped across to Camp Shanks, New York in February of '44. We went to England for five months before we went into Europe in July.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was that crossing like, the Atlantic crossing?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Rough. Because we took a northern course, and it was very storm. You've probably seen these storms on -- in those oil derricks in the North? Well, we went through that. One of them. On the 16th of February was the worst day. And we were in the lead of the convoy. There was destroyers out in front of us, but we couldn't even see them then. The battleship Nevada was on our port, and there was an aircraft carrier back there, and there was ships as far as we could see. And as far as I know, we never had any sound of submarines or activity or anything, but the sea was really rough. Our boat was just bobbing like this, where the battleship, the waves were going right over the deck of it. I was glad to get out of that storm.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you make it okay? Did it get to you? Any seasickness?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Oh, I -- I didn't get sick then. I got sick the first -- the first day when I got up, I didn't go to eat breakfast. And the second day I was supposed to pull guard duty, and I had to go down and -- to chow, to eat, first, you know, before the regular ones did. I went -- went down there, and the smell just got to me. I couldn't take it. So I went back up on deck, and somebody brought me a sandwich to eat up there. That was the only time. But I got sick then, but... So we -- we docked in Scotland, Glasgow, and -- on a Tuesday, 22nd of February. We stayed on the boat until Saturday morning, have transportation. So we would -- left the boat, went to a terminal, got on a train, and traveled all day to southern England. And I don't know; someplace along the line, some big city we went through -- I don't know what it was -- they come on and gave us some English food. These pies, like --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: -- those meat pies that they have.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: When the train pulled out of the station, the windows opened. I'll bet you 75 percent of that stuff was on the -- on the wind. That's bad to say about the English, but we just weren't up to that. And I found out I could go a day without a dinner, you know? In fact, I could go several days without a dinner. So as I say, we -- we trained in England for five months. They even built -- our division even built a rifle range. We got permission from the landowner, so we piled some dirt in the -- up here to protect the guys in the pit, but we had no backstop. Well, there's an airport about a mile away, and when we tried it out, we had to rearrange things. Of course, the engineers are to know, but our division, they had to put a big back -- back, to catch the bullets back there. And of course, they paid this farmer for the -- the land. Well, we had to pay England 50 cents a day for every American that was on the -- on the island.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's the first I've heard that.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And we -- we -- we wasn't on small problems, you know, with our tanks and artillery. And we couldn't go through pasture fields, you know. But they had stone walls encompassing the fields, you know. How does a tank get in there? Drives through, knocks the rocks off. And you'd have to go back the same way, take another exit. So that cost the government a lot of money. They're probably still paying.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with the British people before you went to --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Yeah. I -- I went on pass a couple times, you know. And we -- in our -- in our hut -- we had Quonset huts, and the one fellow, he was a sergeant in the -- another platoon or something. But he -- he was pretty old, and he did jobs down around the mess hall and stuff, working there, you know. And he wasn't out on the line anymore. But when he got out -- when he come back from the mess hall, he'd bring coffee and food and stuff. So we had a regular set-up in our -- our hut. And one Sunday some of the guys went to town, and they met some English fellows, and they brought some back to camp. And they brought them up to our hut to get some coffee and stuff, and somebody mentioned about how -- asked the Canadians how they felt about the English. They (needed) a very good reply. They said of all the food that America and Canada sends over there, when they go over there, they got to eat the English food. They were... So we were good friends. But then when we went to -- to the Continent, we went in, in July, on Utah Beach. Of course, that was taken, but the break-through at -- at -- hadn't occurred yet. But shortly after that, it broke through, and then we were designated Third Army, with Patton, and we turned towards the -- the port Cherbourg.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And Brittany -- and Brest. And it was small -- small towns along there, and they had some fortifications, and some we by-passed and all to get -- get to Brest. And we got to Brest, and we were supposed to attack that next day. But then we got information that some of the pockets that we passed up to get to Brest were coming in behind us; said a couple hundred Germans. So we -- we had to attack back that way, and we captured, I think, 1400 prisoners.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: The first day in combat. Well, I think the -- really, the first big day was August 1st. You know, we had some snipers and stuff like that, and going through a town, and we had -- somebody had to get off, and we got the convoy through town, and they had to mop up the -- the town, you know. But the first one was August 1st. We -- we went through a town; I think the name was Pontorson. The Fourth Armored Division was taking the town, and was finishing up taking that town. And we passed through and went down the road, and the Germans hadn't set up yet. So some of them were -- I was in the Third Platoon, so I was back in the column. And these guys were walking there, and they were -- had their hands over their head, and they were bleeding, because, you know, the guys were shooting at them until they gave up. And they were marching back, and we kept going forward. And then a plane came, a 47 come in, and -- and strafed an area up at the head of our column. By the time we got -- well, we were firing at every hedgerow and everything else, to keep them down. We didn't see many, but it was just like a Wild West show ____ half-tracks. And a couple guys got -- got hit. And we got to where this plane had got -- dived down to strafe. It was an 88 that hadn't got it set up yet. And I went by it, and I was not as far away from it as that house over there. That's the first 88 I saw that close up. And at the same time the hedgerow along the side, machine guns were knocking it, you know, right on through there. So we got through, and on the hill, and set up. Next company came through I think was headquarters, or some other company, and they had to dismount and fight their way through. So that was a Wild West show. But several of the guys got hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you were feeling and thinking on that first day?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I was just thinking -- I -- and I was on the machine gun on the half-track. So you're a little bit more exposed. But I was lucky, I guess. Especially around that 88. But we -- we had a couple bad -- first of October, we had a real bad day.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Approximately. You don't need the -- I don't need the exact city.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It was still in France. We had taken the proper -- I mean, taken the territory. And see, we - we'd sort of spearhead an advance, and hold it, or wait till our infantry division comes in. The infantry division has more people than we have, you know, but we have the -- the motorized unit, tanks and all. They come in and hold it, and we pull back in reserve, or go someplace else, you know. Well, the Germans took the -- took the charge right back from the 35th Division, and so we had to go that day, and there was supposed to be 32 battalions of artillery in our support. The ____ forest, it was. So we come over a skyline, like this, and the Germans could see us coming, and they threw everything at us. And the guy in the -- in the back of our half-track, Picard (ph), his helmet came off. So he opened up the back door, and he run back to get it and pick it up. And he was running to get in the half-track, and the half-track back there said it was a shell hitting after he picked up the hat and followed him down the hill. Over to our right, the First Platoon got a direct hit and killed -- there was two guys, I think, that survived that. The driver, but I don't think he was ever back in combat; he was shook up. He hit -- the radio operator sat behind the driver, and the gas tanks are right there. And the platoon sergeant, he was fighting the fire, and he got -- got killed, you know, trying to get the rest of them; get the guys out.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How big a crew was there on a half-track? Three men?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Oh, a 12-man crew on a half-track?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Twelve, and then the driver would be 13.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: If we had a full squad, yeah.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And the half-tracks -- the headquarters half-track in each platoon had a 50 on it, and you had the officer there, and a platoon sergeant, and a squad leader, and the rest of them. But the rest of them had 30-calibers. But that October 1st, we found a tank destroyer knocked out, and took the 50 off of it, and put it on our half-track. So we had a 50 on ours, and a 30 in the ____. So later on... I won't tell you all the facts, but -- because a lot of them I've forgotten. But if you want to know about my prison experience?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: -- whatever you -- you would like to share. And I have plenty of time, so you can talk.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, we -- we fought along. As I say, we went to -- to Brest, and then we had to go back and pick up the Germans. Then they decided that they needed more than one division to attack Brest, and they took several divisions to attack Brest. And they lost a lot there. So when they went down toward the other port at L'Orient, they figured they would just outpost that and leave it like that. So we outposted there until another division come from overseas, the 95th Division. And when the 95th Division come in, we were -- our platoon was back in reserve, and we heard excitement, so we had to go up. And they -- when the Germans saw a new outfit in there, they -- they counterattacked. And we lost a lot there, but we got it straightened around. And then after a few days we moved on across France, and we got to Nancy, France, and we had a lot of... Because it wasn't -- we didn't go through Paris. That's other outfits went through Paris. We by-passed Paris. We went to Paris later on. But it wasn't -- there wasn't much fighting across France in the southern sector there, below the First Army front there, and -- till we got to Nancy and Metz, and... We were down around the Saar River when we -- in December, when the break-through occurred, so we had to hole up there. And then, when they wanted Patton to bring his troops up, why, it's -- the Fourth Armored was up north of us, so they -- that was the first one that went up, Fourth Armored Division. And then we went up; the Sixth Armored Division moved up through Bastogne.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, I was around Worten (ph), there, when I got... On the second day out, we were in a woods, and we got -- most of us just woke up, you know, and we could hear the Germans in another woods across the road. And the first mortar shell hit there a foot and a half from me, and it ripped my leg, shattered my leg, and got in the other one. The medics patched me up -- they called for the evacuation medics to pick me up, and the medics couldn't get up the road. The Germans wouldn't let them up the road. So eventually I got hung up with the Germans.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did they have to leave you behind, or how did you get --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: They carried me out to the back of this woods to wait on the --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: The medics, to pick me up. And then I -- I heard that they -- they couldn't get up the road. So our company jeep was there, with the driver, and they put me in the front seat of that. And then a mortar barrage came in as our troops were moving out at the time, and we had to wait until that subsided. And there was an officer there from -- the captain, I think, from A company, and in this mortar barrage he got nicked in the arm. So he and the guy -- the fellow that was with me, standing with me talking to me, he got it in the cheek, you know? It burned, but it didn't break any bones, you know. So he and the captain jumped on the back of the jeep; we made a run for it up this road. And we hit the -- hit the road, we got stuck in the ditch, and there was a lot of snow, and even a jeep couldn't get out. And there was a house on this side of the road, a farmhouse, and they run to the farmhouse. And the driver, Parrish (ph), carried me into the thing. And there was some other troops in there, I don't know from --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And medics there, too, so they did some more patchwork on me. And when I -- when they were finished, I asked where this captain and sergeant were, and they said, "Well, they took off in the jeep that was there." And they said they'd be back for me. I'm still waiting. But they -- they were firing back and forth with the Germans, you know, and the road -- there was a little bit of a recess, you know, from the road. And there was an officer; he said -- you know, told the guys to start taking off down there, covering that while we're firing at them. I wasn't, but they were. So later ____ (2 seconds) said, "Come in; it's getting dark." So we had to take cover. We found a entrance to a potato bin in the basement. You know --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: So we got -- went through the trapdoor and got down in the basement. And I think there was about eight or ten of us left. And this -- of course, I think I was the only one that was wounded like that, so they had to help me. And somebody started to sneeze or cough. I heard that, and the Germans were up above, and they heard it. So they threw a grenade in the room. And this officer thought they'll find the trapdoor and throw grenades in there, so he -- he called up to them, and so we -- he surrendered us to the Germans. And I don't know why, but a German hit me so hard he knocked me down; hit me in the jaw. It cracked for years. Never bothered me, but I don't know what it was. And so they -- they marched us quick -- the guys had to carry me -- right to this woods across the road. We went for quite a while, and we stopped at a -- probably a command post. And I don't know if I passed out, or if I fell asleep; I don't know how much time elapsed. But when I woke up, there was other soldiers there, prisoners, and then they started marching us. And I -- I recognized one that was in the Second Platoon, he and his brother. Their names were Phillips. They were from Mississippi or something. And the one guy was meaner than the other. And I think that the good guy got killed before that, Arthur; and this -- I forget what this guy's name was, but he was a mean one, I guess. I -- I couldn't picture him being captured, but he was, and there was an officer with him, but I didn't know the officer. They -- they changed officers quite often in the war. But I saw his name in the POW magazine, and I contacted him, and I invited him to our reunion, B company reunion. This wasn't a POW thing; it was a POW - it was our B company reunion we've had ever since '46. And he sounded like he would like to go, and then he never showed up. But we kept his name on the -- on the roster, and we'd send an announcement out each year. And it's a couple years later he called, and wanted to know where the thing was. He would like to go or something. He lived in Arkansas. And he told me once, he says, "Oh, it's too far." So he never did show up until -- When was it?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: No, that's all right. That's... I've got lots of tape.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: His son -- his son brought him.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And he was pretty old. He was a farmer.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And he had a lot of land, and he just didn't have time, I guess, to --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: -- to come. And I think he passed away now. But he did get to one; his son brought him. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were any other prisoners -- when you were captured, any other prisoners abused? You mentioned that they -- a German hit you.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, I -- I -- I don't know ____. I know he hit me.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: He just hauled off and hit you, huh?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Yeah, well, I was -- I had to -- I was standing right -- I was standing on one leg against the building. And I don't know. Believe me, if I -- because my name was Moncrief instead of Schnartz.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Then you ended up in the prison -- well, tell him how you --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: -- from that point on, yeah, after --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: ____ they marched us, and, of course, they had to take turns carrying me. And I -- we saw a lot of tiger tanks setting in the - you could see the silhouette of the barrels and stuff. We'd gone this road, and we seen a farm wagon. So they got the farm wagon, they put me on it, and another guy or two that they put on, and they pulled us down there. And there was a little house, and they stopped there; it was like a aid station set up. And they dropped me off there, and I don't know if they dropped anybody else. I think somebody else was dropped off there. And the other guys marched on. I don't know where they went. Well, they -- they cut off my -- my shoe, because my foot was swollen so much it was cutting off the circulation. Then the next day they put me on a ox-cart, a little ox-cart, by myself. And I don't know who was driving. I don't know if it was an ox in the front of it or -- or what, but -- I never saw that. I was in the back of this thing. And we're going down the road, and artillery's coming in. And one time the guy stopped, and I think he must have jumped out in the ditch or something. And then he come in. And I'm trying to hold my leg up, because this ox-cart, you know, is just bouncing like hell. And that was an awful ride on that thing. And we came to another house, aid station or something, and they took me in. I didn't get any medication or any food in there, but I waited for other transportation. And the next was a bus. They put me in this bus, and there was some Germans on it. In fact, I was the only American, so I was the last one off after the -- after they got there. They let the stove burn out, you know. It got pretty cold there. I was the last one off. They put -- they took me in, they put me on a table, and they looked at it, and then took me off the table and put me back on the floor. I didn't know what the score was. Finally they came and picked me up and took me to another room, and they started to strap me down. And they put me to sleep, and they operated on my leg. Of course, I didn't see it then. But then they had it bandaged up, and the next time I stopped someplace, why, they took me in there to change the dressing, you know, and when they lifted that leg up, I had two holes on each side of the shinbone about that long and about that wide. And I said, "Oh, don't -- don't drop it; it will break -- break off." You know. They had to leave that open to drain, you know, for the infection. They didn't have penicillin that does that. So I moved on to -- well, I finally got into a regular hospital. It was up in the mountains. I got there by railroad car. I was in a ____ (3 seconds), but I was in a litter, you know? And I was the last one off there. And I was in a ward, oh, there must have been 20 guys in there. And they brought food in. There was a plate of potatoes like that, and a hunk of meat, and I couldn't eat it all. And I hadn't eaten for several days. Well, the next day, they -- they took me and they put me in another room with two other Americans. It was on a different floor. And who they had working for them was German -- I mean Russian POWs. They were carrying people around, you know. And we couldn't -- we tried to talk to them, but we didn't make sense. We couldn't talk Russian, but we made motions about, you know, the Germans and the Americans and the Russians, you know. So we were in this little room, three beds. The one fellow was from the Seventh Armored Division, Ted Shriver. And I used to keep in touch with him -- he lived in Philadelphia -- but I haven't for years. I don't know what happened to him. The other guy, from the 35th Division, I can't remember his name. So then the lady that took care of us, she brought soap and books from home. She could talk English, you know. Was very nice. And she told us that we were going to move out, and that there was another American. There was four of us. So we -- they put us on this -- they call it an Italian train, a hospital train. And it made stops different places, and German soldiers are getting off at different towns and so forth. And we got to the end of the line. Of course, we didn't know where it was, but it happened to have been in Leipzig, Germany. They stopped the train at night, and we stayed on it until morning. And when they loaded us on the back of a truck, the other guy was an Air Corps fighter pilot that was shot down, and the Germans strafed him with a 20-millimeter in his leg, and they had to amputate the leg down below here. But they -- they folded the skin back and cut it off, and then folded that skin, and -- and sewed it up. And a pus pocket, infection, formed in there. When the doctor at the hospital -- he was a Russian, and I think he was a Polish surgeon, and he was a POW, too. He -- he had to cut the end of that leg off and leave it open, you know, so it would drain properly. Just like my leg was open. They didn't have -- the only bandages they had was little pieces of gauze they put right in there, and the rest of it was tissue paper. And they had it in a sling, like -- like a piece of spouting or something, you know, with a brace and a crossbar, so I couldn't turn it. And this Polish doctor, when he looked at it once, he put a cast on it. Well, he did some work on it, and then he put a cast on it. And I figured, How are they going to dress that thing with a cast on it? And I found out: They just got holes in the damn thing. But they -- they had another doctor there who was an Italian, and he was about as good as a barber, I think. And he let -- he let this one here heal too fast. And they would come and take my temperature, and I had a -- well, I had a temperature that was almost 41, which is about a hundred and five or six degrees Fahrenheit. And they looked all over to see what the problem was. Well, they found -- up here they found a big -- above the bandage they found a big welt, and they lanced that open. Well, there was an American doctor there at that time, and he was holding me on the table. He said, "Well, look back there." I said, "Let's see what they're doing." And they lanced that open, and it was so thick they had to dig it out. You know, you'd think that the pus would just --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: -- run out. I got better after that, but I was a sick dog for a couple days.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Tell him about what happened the one night when they -- okay.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, this hospital was only two floors. And it wasn't much longer than this house. Well, it was maybe twice as long, but not too wide. I'd say -- they told me that on the first floor it was all Russians; on the second floor there was anything and everything. You know, Americans, Canadians, Australians, Indians. They had air raid sirens when there was bombing raids in the area, and if you wanted to, if you were able to, you could go to the basement of the building next door to this. It was some kind of a factory or something, but they had a basement. No basement under us. So some of them did, you know, when the alarm was on. The British would bomb at night, and the Americans would bomb during the day. And if they bombed Leipzig, we'd hear it, because it wasn't that far away, you know. But when we went in there, this -- this one guy was loaded on the -- the fourth guy of our foursome, the fighter pilot, he saw the railroad yard there, and he said, "They're going to hit this thing sometime." Well, finally, in April, they did. The English bombed it at night. When the alarm sounded, you know, some guys took off, but I'm laying there with this leg cast. And... I've lost my thought. They...

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, as I say, the alarm was sounded. And then I saw the flares, and the English dropped flares over their target. And I said, This is it. And you could hear the bombs coming down. And some of them would go off, and some of them sounded like duds; nothing, you know. And there was so many duds, I think there couldn't be that many. And I figured out that they must be time bombs, and that's what they were. They'd come down, and then they would go off later. The raid was probably over in 20 minutes to a half-hour, and these things were going off almost to daylight. You know, there'd be a period of time of maybe a half-hour or 45 minutes or something, nothing, and you'd figure it's all over. And then, boom, and you'd hear the... Well, the glass was all out of the building; the walls were cracked; some shrapnel hit the sink in the dressing room, and it cracked it right in half. How I got out, I don't know. But I had this leg cast, and I found myself under the bed for some protection. ___ (3 seconds) when I tried to get out, I fell on the floor, so I lay there for -- till the thing was over. Next day, they brought in a guy that was shot down from one of the lead planes, and he couldn't figure out how they missed it. They didn't know that hospital was there. He said, "I don't know how we missed it." I said, "I don't know either." So shortly after that, the -- the German guards took off, and these guys went out to the railroad and picked up boxes and stuff. They were bringing back these bottles of saccharin tablets. There must have been millions of those, and I don't know what else. I -- I couldn't walk; I didn't go out. But a few weeks after, why, they gave me some -- well, it just finally healed up. They gave me some crutches. So I -- I went out, and I went down the steps. I could see the outside, you know. And I could see planes flying over, our planes, over the city of Leipzig, and I said, Well, they're getting close. So I went back. And then they said that the -- the Germans declared Leipzig a free city, and so they wouldn't bomb it anymore, and the 69th Division came in. And the first truck that came there, I was on it. But I should have been in an ambulance.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, the little bit that you got.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: We -- we didn't have much food. And it was mostly like a soup, and there was nothing to flavor it or nothing, you know. They were supposed to give us POW packages, you know, from the United States, but we only got them a couple times. And when you got them, you had to divide them with a couple other guys, so that didn't go long. And if -- what they did with the cans, they'd punch a hole in it so you couldn't keep it; you had to eat it. Couldn't keep it for... I don't know how any of us could attempt an escape, you know. I know I couldn't. And so...

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were you able to keep up -- obviously you were able -- you knew how the war was going when you saw the planes, but before that, were you able to get much war news?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: No. We didn't get much war news. You know, you've seen some of these movies where they have a radio, and they pick up broadcasts? We didn't. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Probably a little hard to --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: We were just out in the dark.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, once before that I woke up, and I wasn't awake but a short while, and there was a hell of an explosion over on the other side of the building, I thought. And my first reaction was to get out of bed. And this leg cast, I just went so far, and I thought, I'll wait and see what happens. Well, I found out that it was an ammunition train blew up on the railroad tracks out there. And that was a hundred yards or so from the building, but it sounded -- felt like it hit the side of the building. All the glass came out of the building. Guys got cut that were over in that section. But then in this bombing thing, how I got out of that bed, I don't know. So they -- as I say, I got in the back of a two-and-a-half-ton truck, and I'm holding this leg, and we traveled quite a ways till we came to a field hospital. And there were some tents there, but there was a building there, a hospital. So they dropped us off on a tent, and they processed us, and the guy heard that I was from the Sixth Armor, and he says, "I saw your outfit down the road today." And I said, "Yeah. Why didn't they get here sooner?" So we -- we stayed in this tent for -- for a while, and then after dark they came and said that we were moving out. So I went out to get on the truck, and an officer saw me and he raised hell. He says, "You should have been in an ambulance." I said, "I wanted out." So he put me in the cab of that truck instead of in the back of the truck, and I rode with the driver. And I didn't know where we were going, but we went to an airfield. Got to the airfield, you know, late at night. They put us in a tent, and they woke me up about five in the morning and give me a shot. Probably penicillin, which I'd never had before. And then around seven or eight o'clock or something like that, they told us to go down in the tent and get our food. Well, I got a mess here. I'm going through the damn line with these crutches, and I hit a stone. Out I went. An officer saw that, and he chewed the guys out that -- the attendants there, the aides. They were supposed to get my breakfast for me. So they -- I went to sit down; they brought me breakfast. And I thought we would be taking off, you know. All day -- noon, we went and ate again. It was late afternoon, they finally said we're going to take off. Didn't know where we were going, but we took off. And they landed -- they landed ____ (20-second silence in audio file) someplace in France. I don't know if it was around Paris or where. We never got off the plane. And then we took off again, and we went to England, to an airfield in England. And then from there we went to a hospital, 103rd Hospital, and I was there for a couple weeks, and eating their food I had a bad time with diarrhea. Then we got on a plane. We flew to Scotland, Glasgow airport there, and they -- they put you in a stretcher and blanket and tie you all in, and then they take you to the plane and put you in the straps. And the first stop was in Iceland, refuel, and they fed us. When they opened that door, it was cold. It was warm in that thing. But... We had milk to drink; that was the first time. The next one was Newfoundland. We stopped in Newfoundland, and then stopped in -- landed in Long Island, Mitchell Field, Long Island. And then they loaded us on ambulances, take us to the hospital. And it was a woman driver, and I says, "Let me out; I'll walk."

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: "Let me out." After all he'd been through. Would you like a cup of coffee --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: -- or a cup of tea? No?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And so they processed us then, and one officer said, "POWs, we try to get them close to home, if possible." He says, "There's two in Ohio, one in Cambridge" -- and I knew that -- "and one in" --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: -- "in Cleveland." And I didn't know that. And I said, "Well, Cleveland's closer than Cambridge to Canton." So I said, "I'll take Cleveland." He said, "Well, I -- I can't promise you, but we'll try." And there was a guy in the ward next to me, and he was from Michigan, and he wanted to go that way. They took him out to Iowa. Of course, he wasn't a POW, see. So I'm at Crile Hospital. They -- well, on the way they stopped at Pittsburgh and left off a fellow there, and something happened to the plane; they had to do some repair on it. So they put us in the dispensary there, but they couldn't keep us there overnight. They had it for emergency, you know. So they put us on a bus and took us into Pittsburgh, in the old Marine hospital. So we thought the next day we would be going back, you know. Well, I guess the plane wasn't ready, and we stayed there for -- till the afternoon, and then, when they wanted to load us on the bus, not everybody was there. They had to drive around and stop at the bars and get the rest of the guys.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: The ones that were able to get around.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And then get back there, and then we landed in Cleveland. Two of us got off; one was ambulatory, and myself. They had an ambulance and a car. The ambulance with two guys in it, and a car with one guy for -- for two people that could have rode in the -- in an ambulance or whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Is that when you finally saw your family, when you got back to Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Of course, I wrote them when I was in England, but I wasn't there long enough to get an answer. And then when I got to the States I called them, and when I got to Cleveland I called them and told them I was there. Then they -- their friends gave them gas coupons so they could come up to see me, because my dad didn't have but a three or something. And that weekend I came home -- well, I didn't -- wasn't even issued any clothes yet. But I could go home, but in the ward I was in, 29, on the one side it was all officers, and -- I would say A side. On B side the private rooms were all officers, but the people in the back were enlisted men. Some officer heard my folks was going to take me home for the weekend, and he gave me some clothes to wear. I didn't wear the bars with that, but I had the officer's shirt and pants on. And that house was like Grand Central Station that weekend. More people in that house than if I had died, I think. But...

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you were -- after you were captured, how long did it take your family to find out that you were actually a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, they -- I never saw the -- the telegram until after they passed away.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: She had a -- she got a telegram from --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Missing in action. And I was listed on our company records, Missing in action.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: And they -- they never did let her know, his mother know, that he was a prisoner.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: They never did inform you until you let them know that you weren't in --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, see, this -- this hospital was such a small --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: They didn't get food, they didn't get any communication, or nothing. You know, big stalags, big prison camps, Red Cross would come there, and they -- they would communicate, you know, with letters and stuff. But this was a lost sheep.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you were -- were you able to write any letters at all, or try -- I mean, try to write, anyway?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I didn't have any paper or pencil. Nothing.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: But as I say, you know, there was only 50 or 60 on that second floor, until they had to evacuate another hospital, and -- from the Russian advance. And that's when our American doctor come in there, too, then, and two other fellows. And there was a bunk, there was an aisle, then another bunk, an aisle, a bunk. And when they brought those guys in, they had to eliminate an aisle. You'd have two beds together, and then an aisle here, and then two more beds together. You know. So the guy on this aisle, on the -- on the -- it wasn't much of an aisle -- his name was Umstott (ph). His dad was president at Timken Roller Bearing Company in Canton, Ohio. And you heard me say that I was from Canton, Ohio. And the guy on my right, which was butted up against me, he was from the Second Division, and he was from Canton, Ohio; Italian fellow.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Three guys from Canton, a little hick town. (Laughing) I didn't mean it. But the odds on that was pretty good. But I can't remember the Italian fellow's name. And Umstott, I -- when I was home once, I -- I called, and he was home, and I -- I went up to see him, and met his father. My brother worked for Timken's for almost 45 years, so he was aware of Umstott. But anyway, I -- I don't know; it was --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you have any -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: When I was discharged in February, I moved back to Cleveland, because there was somebody -- somebody waiting there for me.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I don't know. I ought to tell that football story.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were you -- were you dating at all when he was --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: I didn't meet him -- I didn't meet him until he was at Crile Hospital. And I always wanted to go there, because I heard so much about it. And he happened to get a pass to go to a football game on a Friday night.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, I would go home on weekends.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: But I was supposed to have surgery on a Monday. So I couldn't go home on the weekend, but I could go into town. And a fellow and I in the ward wanted to -- went to the football game. It was Massillon against Cathedral Latin. So I -- I went there, and... We could get in free, you know, in uniform. Of course there was some sections you couldn't go in; you had to go on. So I went in this -- it was this lower section, you know.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And there was a woman setting over here, and we come in -- this was empty; this row was empty. I come in, and I says, "Are these seats taken?" And she said, "Well, these two are." And I said, "Okay." So we sat down, my buddy and I. Pretty soon two other women come in, and they sat down. And we got to talking, and we got to talking. That was November 2nd. She -- the girls wanted to see the Crile, but they had to know somebody there, I guess, to get in.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: So they -- they were going to come on Monday. Well, Sunday, I'm thinking -- they -- they didn't do any prep work on me, and I -- what's the score? I checked with them, and the operation was canceled. So I called her. I said, "The operation's canceled; you don't have to come." They came anyway. And I think they stopped at three bakeries, and they bought enough to cover the whole bed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: We brought so much stuff. Really, you know, they had German fellows there, in the PX and so forth, with big POWs on their backs, working there --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: -- you know. That was amazing. And then that hospital was primarily for plastic surgery, because that's where they wanted --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: -- not entirely. But they had a big section for it, yes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: And that's why he was there, to kind of put some more flesh or something on that shinbone.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, they took -- cut out the scar tissue on the other ones, and they didn't have enough skin, so they took a skin graft from my leg and covered the one area. Didn't take too good, but...

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: But he had been in Crile for nine months.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When did you finally get back to the States, then? Was that...

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: So I was there from May until -- middle of May until --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Actually that's when you were discharged?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: From the hospital and from the Army?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I was a free man, except for one thing.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: No, as I say, I met her on November 2nd.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: February 14th I gave her a ring.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Our first son was born on the 7th of October.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: He tells everybody that. Four years later.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Four years later. All right. The official --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: He was premature. He lives in Florida.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Before you were captured, did you have any close buddies in the outfit?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: The closest ones are from the old 535th, you know. We were in training together, and when we joined the Sixth, we were together. The fellows in the Sixth were a little older than we were. They were up -- some of them were up in their thirties. There were a couple guys that were forty. I -- the one guy told me in England that they asked him -- you know, he was forty then. They asked him if he wanted to go to a different outfit. You didn't have to go in the front line if you were age forty. He says, "I'll go with them." That was Kimball.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Kimball. Yeah. But we've had these reunions every year since the --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Because they didn't know what happened to me.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: They didn't -- they didn't send any announcement to my old address or anything. And you know where the first reunion was?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And -- you know. Of course, when I came up here, I didn't have much to rub together.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And I didn't have a car. I only had a wife.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: She was working, though. And I finally got a job, and...

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: During the war, did you and your buddies, did you get a chance to do much for entertainment, for fun, or what -- you know. Would you have breaks from combat or training?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, training? Well, we had some time, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Get some shows in England at all? Did you get any shows when you were in England?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I never saw a USO show until a few years ago. I mean -- what I'm saying is a production USO show.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: When we were on our way from the Third Army front up to the First Army front, you know, at the -- at the break-through, we went through this Belgian town. We stayed there: Bellefontaine. And we saw a jeep coming in, and it had a couple entertainers on it. Mickey Rooney and some other guy; I don't know his name. And they put on a little skit for maybe ten, 15 minutes. That wasn't much of a USO show.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I didn't consider it that. And then one time we saw Marlene Dietrich, but this was before -- this was in France there someplace, before we got over. And she was just there, you know. No -- no show to it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: And where did you see Bob Hope?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Wait a minute. Until the Crile Hospital.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: It was just Hope and Crosby. And Hope was out there first, and he, you know, mouthed off a while, and then Bing come out and... I don't think the thing lasted 20 minutes. You know, there was no dancing girls, or no show, I consider. Now, they had a show in -- in Columbus, what, about four years ago?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And I consider that the first and only USO show I saw.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Yeah. And it was very good.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Crosby sang a few songs, I assume, in the 20 minutes; right?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did Crosby sing a few songs?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I think he did. He probably sang one or two, yeah. But as I say, Hope was out there longer.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: He was out there before Bing came on.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did you lose any buddies when you were overseas in France?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: You've got to show him those cards, honey. He would be interested in seeing those cards. Turn it off.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Every day, morning reports all the --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And he's got those. And then some guy made copies of them. I -- he had it handwritten; I typed them up.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: But what date should he look, where you lost so many men?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: I know you have never seen anything like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: No. I've seen after-action reports, but I've never seen that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: The after-action reports, yeah, exactly. They have --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: This was daily reports, and it -- it -- and even said about the mood of the fellows.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah. No. I've never seen anything like that.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: In November. KI means killed in action.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: See, it gives the name, and their -- and their rank or whatever.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Serial number. What happened; killed in action, and the date. Lightly wounded. Severely wounded. I guess that's what he meant by it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I think that's -- yeah. I think that's exactly...

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Killed in action. And, see, this is when the wounded is evacuated.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And if they returned to our company, it gives the date they --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: -- returned. And if there's no date there, they never came back.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, here's some that were wounded, but they remained on duty.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: There's several of those. Let me get back here to the...

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: And show him where you're listed.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, this card and the next couple is when we hit the Battle of the Bulge

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So all those -- well, you know, I guess you don't know that all those guys were captured.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, some of those that were missing in action, they -- they came back. They got --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Or wounded, I guess, and captured, on April 1st, 1945?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And a few years ago, couple years ago...

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: What were you going to say?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Some fellow got in touch with us; through the Sixth Armored Division or something, he got in touch with us. They referred him to us. He was looking about his father. His father was listed as a missing in action.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And then later he got a telegram, or his mother got it or something, that he was killed in action. And he couldn't figure out. One is missing, and one is killed, the same day. Well, he -- he was only four years old or something when he... So he'd -- he'd been coming to our reunions, and picking up information, and he thought he would go on over and visit his father's grave.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And he's taken dirt from their home and took it over there, and laid on the --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: -- on the grave, and brought some of that back. And he's real involved with it, you know. What's his name?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: I can't think of it at the moment.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Here. Give me the thing, and I'll find it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Well, yeah, it looks like a long list of guys missing in action and killed in action on --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, see, a lot of these -- lot of these -- some of these missing in action, then they show up.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: They got with other outfits, see.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: But January 4th must have been a pretty intense day.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: That was a pretty bad day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Yes. That's right. Well, the Battle of the Bulge was the worst.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Uh-huh. George Connor, killed in action.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: That's ____ came to one of our reunions. Her brother had been killed. You know, Cathy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: She went up to Noel about his -- who was with his -- her brother, and she was interviewing all these fellows, and we didn't know whether she was going to write a book, or -- or what.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And she kept coming. You know --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: She kept coming to the reunions, thinking somebody else will be there that knew her brother. And finally, last year is the first that she didn't come back. Then I heard she got married, so maybe --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Yeah. I mean, she's -- she's getting --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: -- to be a pest. She was getting to be a pest.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: We had the reunion in -- in Akron.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Yeah. We hosted it when it was in the Holiday Inn on Route 18.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Yeah. Next to 71, there. And you know, some people fly, in the airport, and we said that -- the Akron airport or the Cleveland airport.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, we got stuck by -- having to go both -- both ways

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, this -- this one day we had to pick them up at Cleveland airport, and it was this babe.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And shortly -- Katie. And shortly after, we had to pick up the colonel. And of course, the colonel's with his wife and the luggage, and she has a walker.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: He's just as alert... Oh, you never met anybody like that. And his name is the same as ours.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: He wrote a couple of books, and we're listed in there as to how we met, and...

sp.speaker: Mrs. Moncrief
sp.p: Big story. But I knew you would be interested --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Here's that officer I was telling you about, Kornegay (ph). See, they just had him missing in action, but when I typed these cards, I knew he was a POW, so I --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, he wasn't in the camp with me, no. He got captured...

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: The same day that I was, but at a different time.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Here's this Jack fellow I told you --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: His brother got killed, but this guy was captured the same night as --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: The one question I usually ask, just to see if there's anything we haven't covered, when you think about World War II, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: I guess that bombing raid stands out more than anything.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Because you didn't know when one of those damn things was going to hit. And I --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Pretty much devastated everything around there.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Of course, I couldn't get out to look at it, but it must have played hell with the railroad yard.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So how close was the hospital to the railroad yard?

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: Well, it -- it couldn't be more than a couple hundred yards. It was right there.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And this -- this fighter pilot, when he come in there, he said, "They're going to hit that place." And I -- I thought of that several times, you know. I said, "Well, they -- they haven't hit it yet. Haven't hit it yet." And I've heard... There was a guy across this aisle from me, you know, in the other row -- he was an Australian -- I guess he was a pilot.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: But he was pretty sick. He had yellow jaundice. He was -- his skin was yellow.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And he had -- well, the doctor come in there once, and they set him up in bed, and a doctor and the aides or something, a couple of them there, and they had a hypodermic needle, and they were jabbing him and drawing off the fluid.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: And I -- I counted up into the teens, but then a lot of them gathered round, and I couldn't finish. I don't know how many. But they were up in the teens, at this damn...

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: You know, most of the guys, like this Umstott fellow that had double pneumonia, they knock out a piece of rib, and they put a tube in there, and they drain. Why they didn't do it with him, I don't know. You know, they tried to take it out then. But in that bombing raid, he died. I guess his heart give out. I don't -- I don't know, but he died that night of the air raid.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Not from the bombing, but simply as --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: -- happened to die that night, and --

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: It was just too much for him, I guess. I don't know what -- what happened.

sp.speaker: Milton M. Moncrief
sp.p: They don't have to do autopsies there.
